transcript:
Header:
Date: 2025-09-11
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Carlos Nguyen (Redwood SE), Aisha Khan (QuantaHealth), Tom Reyes (CTO), Lena Ortiz (SRE), Benji (Data Eng)

Summary: quick run through of this week's POC results. Focus on TTFT and streaming behaviour under variable sequence length and kernel choice. Discussed bandwidth limits causing microburst latency spikes and a proposed kernel hedge. Agreed next steps and owners.

Topics:
- TTFT (time-to-first-token) trends over seqlen buckets
- Streaming handshake and early-response buffering
- Kernel selection tradeoffs and CPU/GPU bandwidth impact
- Tradeoff: small-batch low-latency vs batching for cost

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya: alright thanks everyone for joining, um we'll try to keep to 50 minutes, uh couple updates from our side then go into the new traces.
[00:18] Aisha: sounds good, we've got Tom and Lena on for infra questions and Benji has the sample logs.
[00:24] Carlos: quick note — I pulled last night's run, the TTFT median improved with the new condense-cache setting but the 95 and 99 look noisy, microbursts still there.
[00:35] Benji: yeah uh that's what we saw, the thing is we have a wide distribution of sequence lengths, a lot of short queries and then spikes of 1k tokens; not consistent.
[00:50] Tom: to be clear, our goal is sub-200ms TTFT for chat UI and 99th under 600ms, otherwise product folks will be unhappy, right?
[01:05] Maya: right yes, and we can trade cost. We want to explore whether switching kernels for short sequences buys us that tail without obliterating throughput.
[01:20] Lena: also worth calling out network shaping — our current cloud region applies egress shaping on the dedicated pool; could that explain microbursts?
[01:35] Carlos: possibly. The traces show concurrency spikes aligning with egress throttles. We instrumented K-V cache warmness, though some of the names got munged in the trace — looks like "K-V cash" on the export — so ignore that label.
[01:50] Aisha: funny, yeah the export had weird tokens. But can you explain the kernel hedge again?
[01:58] Carlos: sure. We basically fast-path short sequences onto a different kernel that's optimized for small seq-len — lower startup overhead but worse steady throughput. For the long ones we keep the high-throughput kernel. We can route by observed seqlen or by predicted early token.
[02:15] Tom: is there an extra serialization cost switching kernels mid-request?
[02:22] Carlos: minimal if we route at request start. The tricky bit is streaming and early-response — if we switch kernels after streaming handshake, we might double buffer. There was one test where streaming had handshake jitter and we saw extra 30-60ms.
[02:40] Maya: ok so main questions: does kernel switching reduce 99th? does it hurt median or throughput? and does network/bandwidth shaping dominate?
[02:52] Aisha: our quick read — median improves slightly, 99th sometimes halved in synthetic but in prod-like traces it was mixed.
[03:05] Carlos: and on top of that, when we turned on continuous batching we saved tokens but introduced small batching delay (10-20ms) which affects TTFT; that's the classical latency vs cost tradeoff.
[03:22] Benji: i put a link in the chat to the perf spreadsheet — the microburst bucket is column D, the seqlen histogram is sheet 2.
[03:30] Maya: yeah we saw that. Can you run a trimmed trace where you isolate network egress shaping off? Like ephemeral test cluster with no shaping, just to validate?
[03:40] Lena: we can try but need approval, our security policy wants a scoped test. I'll open the ticket.
[03:46] Tom: also are we seeing differences between hosted and dedicated nodes? We did an earlier comparison but I think the dedicated nodes had less variance.
[03:54] Carlos: dedicated has less fund variance because of isolation, but if the network layer at cloud front is shaping bursts that still shows up.
[04:04] Aisha: one oddity — the tokenized prompt size varies because front-end templates sometimes embed metadata; that changes seqlen distribution. We should normalize or at least bucket by prompt templates.
[04:18] Maya: good point. Benji, can you add a template tag in the traces?
[04:22] Benji: yeah I can, will do.
[04:26] [05:00] Speaker 1: (inaudible) — sorry i missed that — did we try the low-latency kernel with streaming disabled?
[05:08] Carlos: we did, and TTFT was great for short queries but streaming responses (where we really need first chunk) had poorer chunk cadence, so UX got jitter.
[05:22] Aisha: UX is top priority for our team, so chunk cadence matters a lot.
[05:28] Maya: maybe a hybrid: for predicted short queries we route to low-latency kernel but keep streaming handshakes aligned with high-throughput kernel cadence. It's messy but doable.
[05:42] Tom: what's the risk to cost? If we split kernels we might underutilize GPU and raise per-token cost.
[05:50] Carlos: yep worst-case 12-20% unit cost increase if short queries dominate and cannot be batched. But we can counteract with prefix caching and predicted batching.
[06:07] Aisha: speaking of caching, the prefix cache warmness seems low for a lot of queries — is that a primer issue?
[06:15] Carlos: looks like frequent prompt variation nullifies cache. We recommended prompt normalization and selective prefixing.
[06:23] Maya: action: we'll prepare two experiments: (A) kernel hedging by seqlen with routing rules and (B) aggressive prompt normalization plus continuous batching tuning. Run both against the same trace set.
[06:35] Benji: i'll run both and will include the egress-off variant if Lena can provision.
[06:42] Lena: i'll raise the ticket and try to get approval in 48 hours.
[06:47] [20:10] Carlos: on the metrics side, we added a microburst probe that logs per-request network queue times; hooking that up shows egress spikes matching the 99th.
[20:25] Tom: ok so that's a pretty strong signal network is a major contributor. Does Redwood have recommendations for handling network shaping other than re-routing regions?
[20:35] Maya: yes we have a couple: 1) region hedging — route to a sibling region with lower shaping (requires cross-region SLOs), 2) local prebuffering on the client side for streaming handshake, 3) request-level admission to smooth bursts. We'll share a doc.
[20:50] Aisha: can you share sample configs for admission control? That'd be helpful.
[20:55] Maya: yes will include examples.
[21:02] Carlos: also, we think a small tweak to the kernel scheduler that prioritizes first-token paths for predicted short requests could shave 40-70ms at 99th with limited cost impact; it's an engineering change but low-risk.
[21:20] Tom: timeline on that?
[21:24] Carlos: prototype in 2 weeks, but won't be in production until after validation.
[21:30] Maya: ok good. Any blockers?
[21:34] Aisha: need the seqlen histogram and production SLOs — will share by Friday.
[21:40] Benji: i'll update the sheet with template tags and isolated traces.
[21:45] Lena: i'll try to get egress exemption for 48 hours.
[21:50] Maya: perfect — let's recap.
[21:54] Recap: Maya to share perf spreadsheet + notes (due 2025-09-13); Carlos to produce synthetic microburst trace and prototype scheduler change (due 2025-09-16 for trace, two-week proto for scheduler); QuantaHealth to provide seqlen hist and SLOs (Aisha due 2025-09-12); Lena to file egress ticket (due 2025-09-14).
[22:12] Tom: thanks all. Can we aim for a follow up next week same time to look at results?
[22:18] Maya: yes same time next Thursday, I'll send invite.
[22:22] [END]
